candidates.next_evidence: Verify latest HBM revenue mix, fiscal 2026/2027 capacity commitments, customer concentration, HBM gross-margin trajectory, and whether supply is constrained by wafer capacity, TSV/stacking, packaging, or substrate availability.
candidates.node_relation: Direct HBM supplier; announced volume production shipments of 12-high 36GB HBM4 for NVIDIA Vera Rubin and sampling of 16-high 48GB HBM4.
candidates.theme_relation: AI accelerators require high-bandwidth, power-efficient memory close to compute; HBM availability can constrain accelerator platform ramps.
candidates.why_include: Micron is one of the few global HBM suppliers and has direct product exposure to next-generation AI accelerator platforms. HBM requires specialized DRAM process technology, TSV/stacking know-how, packaging coordination, and long customer qualification cycles.

candidates.next_evidence: Track CoWoS capacity additions, allocation by NVIDIA/AMD/Broadcom/custom ASIC customers, capex mix for advanced packaging, and any evidence that substrate or tool bottlenecks limit CoWoS expansion.
candidates.node_relation: Capacity controller for leading-edge logic and advanced packaging technologies including CoWoS, InFO, SoIC, and related 3D/chip-stacking platforms.
candidates.theme_relation: Many leading AI GPUs and ASICs require TSMC leading-edge logic plus CoWoS-like 2.5D packaging to integrate compute die with HBM stacks.
candidates.why_include: TSMC is a central capacity gatekeeper for AI accelerator production because wafer capacity and advanced-packaging capacity both matter. Its annual report explicitly links AI demand to leading-edge, specialty, and advanced-packaging investment.

candidates.next_evidence: Look for customer wins, advanced-packaging revenue disclosure, Korea/Arizona capacity milestones, chiplet/HPC package qualifications, and whether Amkor handles meaningful AI accelerator packaging rather than lower-complexity assembly.

candidates.why_include: Amkor states it is strengthening its strategic presence in AI and HPC and describes itself as a global leader in outsourced semiconductor packaging and test services. Its inclusion is justified as a packaging/test capacity candidate, but the direct linkage to HBM stack or CoWoS-equivalent bottlenecks must be proven in later layers.

candidates.next_evidence: Quantify advanced-packaging revenue, HBM customer concentration, order backlog duration, tool lead times, and competitive position versus KLA, Camtek, Nova, and other inspection/metrology vendors.

candidates.theme_relation: HBM and 2.5D advanced packaging require tighter bump, RDL, TSV, overlay, and defect-control processes; metrology and inspection tools can become enabling capacity nodes.
candidates.why_include: Onto is a less obvious but relevant supplier because advanced packaging capacity depends not only on assemblers but also on inspection/metrology tools that enable yields at fine pitch and high stack complexity.

candidates.next_evidence: Check whether HBM-related orders expand materially in 2026, whether customers are Micron/SK hynix/Samsung or OSATs, whether HBM inspection is recurring or tool-cycle driven, and whether revenue remains too small to affect consolidated growth.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Semiconductor test, automation, inspection, and metrology equipment
candidates.theme_relation: As HBM moves to higher stack counts and finer interconnect structures, inspection and metrology of micro-pillars and stacked packages can become a yield and throughput dependency.

memory_update.text: MU should be retained as a direct HBM capacity candidate for the AI HBM/advanced-packaging node; official 2026 disclosure confirms HBM4 production shipments for NVIDIA Vera Rubin.
TSM should be retained as a core capacity-controller candidate because CoWoS and related advanced-packaging platforms are explicitly tied to AI demand and customer capacity planning.
ONTO and COHU are equipment-vendor candidates with direct HBM or 2.5D AI-packaging inspection/metrology evidence; they may represent less obvious chokepoint exposures than memory makers or foundries.
AMKR is a plausible second-order advanced-packaging/test capacity candidate, but later layers must distinguish broad OSAT AI/HPC exposure from true HBM or CoWoS-equivalent bottleneck control.

Not included due to the 5-candidate limit but worth checking in later passes: ASX/ASE Technology, KLAC, CAMT, FORM, ENTG, KLIC, TER, AMAT, LRCX, ASML, BESIY, Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, Kinsus, Disco, and ASMPT. Some are ADR/OTC or non-US primary listings and require listing/liquidity classification.

node: HBM, advanced memory, and advanced packaging
summary: Expanded US-listed universe for the HBM and advanced-packaging chokepoint. The strongest direct candidates are Micron for HBM supply and TSMC for CoWoS/advanced packaging capacity. Second-order but still plausible chokepoint exposures include Amkor as an OSAT packaging/test capacity provider, Onto Innovation as advanced-packaging/HBM process-control equipment, and Cohu as HBM inspection/metrology equipment. This is a research universe only, not a trading recommendation.
